concept.label: Gale–Shapley deferred acceptance algorithm
concept.learning_takeaway: Proposals and provisionally held best offers produce a stable allocation under the specified preference model.
concept.card: In Gale–Shapley deferred acceptance, each proposer approaches their best remaining choice. Each recipient provisionally retains the preferred proposal and rejects others. With strict rankings in the standard one-to-one model, these repeated rounds yield a stable matching.
concept.original_description: algorithm for solving the stable matching problem

concept.label: Boston immediate acceptance mechanism
concept.learning_takeaway: Finalizing first-choice admissions before later rounds makes preference reporting strategically consequential.
concept.card: In the Boston school-choice mechanism described in 2003, schools fill seats permanently in rounds of first choices, then second choices and so on. Later applicants cannot displace earlier admissions through higher priority. Consequently, reporting true preferences is not generally a dominant strategy.

concept.label: Moral hazard in teams
concept.learning_takeaway: Shared observable output with hidden individual actions creates a team-specific free-riding problem.
concept.card: Moral hazard in teams arises when individual actions are hidden but joint output is observable. In Holmström’s model, sharing that output under a balanced budget can leave members with incentives to free ride. The team setting changes the contract-design problem.

evidence.locator: Abstract and Introduction, printed p. 324 / PDF p. 1

relations.note: The introduction explicitly defines the paper’s setting as a multiagent extension of the moral-hazard problem.

concept.label: Relative performance evaluation
concept.learning_takeaway: Peers’ outcomes can supply information useful for designing an individual’s incentive contract.
concept.card: Relative performance evaluation lets a contract use peers’ outcomes alongside an agent’s own performance. In Holmström’s model, comparing agents can provide information useful for incentives. The value of competition therefore depends on its informational role in the contracting problem.

relations.note: The abstract explicitly investigates relative performance evaluation as a scheme to improve incentives using information about peer agents.

concept.label: Tennis service let
concept.learning_takeaway: A qualifying service let repeats that serve while preserving an earlier service fault.
concept.card: Under standard ITF rules, a serve that touches the net and is otherwise valid is a service let. That particular serve is repeated. If it was a second serve, an earlier first-service fault remains; the let does not restart the whole service sequence.

initial_findings.issue: Preferred schools does not specify the mechanism’s highest-ranked remaining choice.
initial_findings.proposed_repair: Say each remaining student points to their highest-ranked remaining school with an available seat; preserve the school-priority rule.
initial_findings.proposed_body: In school-choice top trading cycles, each remaining student points to their highest-ranked school with available seats, and each school points to its highest-priority remaining student. Cycles assign seats; assigned students leave, capacities decrease, and full schools leave. Repeating these steps allocates the seats.

concept.label: Top trading cycles
concept.learning_takeaway: Directed preference-and-priority cycles assign seats simultaneously and remove completed trades.
concept.card: In school-choice top trading cycles, students point to preferred schools and schools point to remaining students with highest priority. Directed cycles assign seats; assigned students leave and capacities adjust. With strict rankings, repeating this process turns cycles into allocations.

concept.label: Top trading cycles
concept.learning_takeaway: Directed preference-and-priority cycles assign seats simultaneously and remove completed trades.
concept.card: In school-choice top trading cycles with strict preference and priority rankings, each remaining student points to their highest-ranked school with seats; each school points to its highest-priority remaining student. Cycles assign seats, remove assigned students, reduce capacities and remove full schools. Repetition completes the allocation.

concept.label: Wheelchair tennis two-bounce rule
concept.learning_takeaway: A wheelchair player may return after two bounces, and the second bounce may fall outside the court.
concept.card: Wheelchair tennis permits a player to return the ball after a second bounce. The first bounce must still satisfy the ordinary court-boundary rule; the second may land outside the court. The adaptation changes return timing while preserving the first-bounce requirement.
